reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: A benign surface (juxtacortical) hyaline cartilage tumour arising beneath the periosteum, favouring the proximal humerus, the small tubular bones of the hand and long-bone metaphyses in adolescents and young adults.
The lesion erodes and saucerises the underlying cortex, producing a well-defined defect with a sclerotic margin and characteristic overhanging periosteal buttresses at its edges.
It is typically small, usually under about 3 to 4 cm; larger surface cartilage lesions should raise suspicion for periosteal chondrosarcoma.
Chondroid matrix mineralisation in a ring-and-arc pattern may be visible within the lesion.
MRI shows lobulated tissue of high T2 signal with peripheral and septal enhancement and, importantly, no invasion of the medullary cavity.
It must be distinguished from periosteal chondrosarcoma and periosteal osteosarcoma, which are larger and show cortical destruction, marrow invasion or a soft-tissue mass.
Marginal en bloc excision is curative and local recurrence is uncommon when excision is complete.
reference.pathophysiology: Periosteal chondroma is a benign neoplasm of mature hyaline cartilage that develops on the surface of a bone, deep to the periosteum and superficial to the cortex. As the cartilaginous lobules enlarge they exert pressure on the underlying cortex, producing the characteristic scalloped cortical erosion (saucerisation) with a reactive sclerotic base and buttressing periosteal new bone at the margins, while by definition the process remains confined to the surface and does not invade the medullary cavity. Histologically it comprises lobules of hypercellular hyaline cartilage that may show mild atypia and binucleate cells, features acceptable in a surface lesion but which contribute to difficulty distinguishing it from low-grade surface chondrosarcoma; IDH mutations may be present as in other cartilage tumours.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs to demonstrate cortical saucerisation with sclerotic margins and periosteal buttressing
MRI to characterise the cartilage and confirm absence of marrow invasion
CT to define cortical scalloping and matrix mineralisation
Assessment of lesion size as a discriminator from surface chondrosarcoma
Biopsy for large or atypical lesions, interpreted with awareness of overlap with low-grade malignancy
Comparison with prior imaging to assess for growth in the skeletally mature
redFlags: Lesion size greater than about 5 cm
Cortical destruction rather than smooth saucerisation
Documented growth in a skeletally mature adult
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, with a low rate of local recurrence following adequate marginal excision and negligible malignant potential.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as periosteal chondrosarcoma, leading to overtreatment, or the reverse leading to inadequate surgery
Confusing it with osteochondroma, which shows corticomedullary continuity
Incomplete excision predisposing to local recurrence
Overlooking marrow invasion on MRI, which would indicate malignancy
